title: Near misses are reportable, including confusion, unclear documentation and training gaps
content:
A.2.11.1.3.2.2.1.2.1.3 defines a third reporting tier for "events that did not result in compromise but may indicate risk," listing social engineering attempts, suspicious emails or messages, "[s]ecurity procedure confusion or errors," and "[t]raining gaps or unclear documentation."

The first two items are conventional threat intelligence — one signer's phishing attempt is usually a campaign against all of them, and only aggregation reveals that.

The last two are the notable ones, because they are not attacks at all. Classifying "unclear documentation" as a reportable near miss treats the framework's own quality as a security variable, on the reasoning that a signer who does not understand a procedure will eventually improvise one — and improvisation under time pressure is what social engineering exploits. The vulnerability is in the document, so the document is what gets reported.

This is standard practice in aviation and clinical safety, where near-miss reporting is the primary source of pre-incident data, and it is unusual to see it written into crypto key management. It only functions in a blame-free reporting culture: a signer who expects to be judged for admitting confusion will not report it, and the tier goes silent while looking healthy.

The Atlas hedges accordingly — near misses "should be reported ... when practical," the only tier without a mandatory clock, which is realistic about enforceability but also makes this the tier most likely to be skipped.
description: Events that caused no compromise but indicate risk — social engineering attempts, suspicious messages, procedural errors — are treated as signal, importing safety-culture practice into key operations.
